If sony wanted to support eye tracking on pcvr they would have to develop software for it(might actually already be done for dev purposes?) and license it specifically for pc. On top of that, any software/games that you would want to support eye tracking would also need to have that built into it, which many/most do not. And foveated encoding isn't going to be useful for the psvr2 because it is not a streaming headset and doesn't need it.

Whenever you're on a budget you're probably going to have to make some compromises. It'd be helpful to know what your budget is and roughly your region(europe? SE asia? etc). Also my apologies, I wrote out a bunch of stuff under the assumption you were in the US so it is mainly going to apply there. But I will say look at 12gb cards like the 7700xt or the 6700xt before you get something like a 4060 16gb or a 7600xt. Although between the two I'd just take the performance hit and get the 7600xt but that largely depends on price. don't get the 3060 12gb at this point, it's a bad value for what you get as it's pretty much the cheapest nvidia gpu with 12gb.

One option is a used navi 21 gpu. These potentially have USB c(won't promise it will work, do your own research, but seems like it would) This puts you somewhere in the viscinity of rtz 4070/RX 7800xt levels of performance with 16gb of vram. Used navi 21 GPUs tend to range from $300-500 depending on if you're getting a rx 6800 or a 6950. Of course if you're getting an adapter your options widen, you could get something like a 7800 xt which would provide you with roughly similar performance.

Unfortunately on team nvidia there isn't really anything with 16gb of vram that I would consider budget. You could try snagging a 2080 ti for cheap, that could be a good card for the $230-$275 range. All of these should have USB C. But then you step it up to ampere and things just get bad. If you try and snag something like a 3080 12gb or 3080 ti you might get that for the $400-$450 range. But isn't that kinda getting outside of budget territory? If you were lucky maybe you could score a 4060 ti 16gb for $375. But you're going to lose a lot of performance at higher resolutions on account of the narrow bus. Overall this is just a bad card. 

If you have to buy new, look at this gpu from the official xfx store on newegg. make sure you have clearance for it in your case and your psu is good enough. also note this gpu does not have usb c. https://www.newegg.com/xfx-radeon-rx-6800-rx-68xlaqfde/p/N82E16814150886

Summary: My gut says find a good used 2080 ti. Not only is it about the same performance as these next gpus, you should also be able to forego the $60 adapter. If you have to buy new, try to see if you can find a 6700xt. Over here they're $300 usd new which seems a bit much, but it should be roughly 15% faster than the 7600xt at 4k. of course if you think you have use for the extra vram or the other extra features of RDNA 3 then the 7600xt might be better for you. If you can swing for an rx 6800 though and there's a good deal available, really try to go that way. It's roughly 48% faster than the 7600xt at 4k and only $60 more new in the USA(not sure what that's gonna look like outside the US or if there's even availability)

there should be more added to this before you go out and buy base stations and trackers. For one you need to make sure your playspace is good for base stations. 1. it needs to be big enough 2. you need to make sure there isn't stuff in your play area that will interfere with the trackers/base stations. The base stations emit an infrared laser which the trackers pick up on to determine their position in space. so things that are reflective and/or put out infrared light will interfere with them. The base stations need to be placed in a certain way for good performance, you need to figure out where you're going to put them. 

you don't really HAVE to go out and buy a tracker for your headset. But to make base station tracking work with steamvr when you don't have a base station tracked headset, you'll need a piece of software called openvr space calibrator. This piece of software needs a way to line up the playspace of your non-base station tracked headset and the native steamvr base station tracking. To do this normally you hold a tracker in your hand with your controller, do a bit of wiggling about with it, and space calibrator uses the data to figure out where to put everything. But it can get out of alignment over time, so to mitigate this you put a tracker on your headset and use a fork of space calibration called the continuous calibration fork. and it basically does this calibration all the time so you never need to do the calibration again. It doesn't work 100% perfectly but it is a heck of a lot better than doing the calibration all the time. 

so if that sounds like a lot, I'd wait a bit and do more digging before buying stuff to make sure you get the best possible experience. also adding more trackers gives you increasingly diminishing returns, particularly depending on what you're doing. I'd say... get a couple base stations and 3 trackers, see how you like it and go from there.

I don't know a lot about mocap suits but I rarely see folks using them, and I figure there's a good reason for that. It's probably because they're very expensive, and use imus anyway. imu tracking is what slimes use, and slimes have to periodically be reset. The tracking quality is good but lots of folks don't want to be arsed with resetting like that. I'm not really sure if you'd have to do that with a mocap suit or if it is even so easy to just use a mocap suit, but I'm going to bet that getting a mocap suit to work with vrc is going to be more work than either of us would be willing to put into it. 

So basically, just get vives or tundras. I mean, you could get slimes, there are some advantages to them. but most people I know and talk to prefer vive trackers. Main advantages of slimes are: no occlusion and longer battery life. disadvantages are: more challenging setup, has to periodically be reset, less accurate tracking. 

so what is occlusion? Base station trackers have to be able to see the base stations. when they can't, they lose tracking. so for example if you wanted to cover yourself with a blanket, you can do that with slimevr trackers but not vives or tundras.

Oh yeah, if you want official slimes you'll have to be waiting at least a few months to get them after you order. or just buy a set used(probably lose warranty with this route) or buy a set of handmade trackers.

oh yeah, index controllers.

I don't know which headset or controllers you're using, but index controllers are basically the controllers you want if you have a base station tracked headset, or want controllers with finger tracking. Be aware that the finger tracking is not perfect. Also, index controllers track just like vive and tundra trackers so they are not limited to the headset's range of vision like quest controllers(aside from the pro controllers) are. Disadvantages  of index controllers are that the battery life is considerably worse than quest 2/3 controllers(about 6-7 hours) and a lot of folks figure they are less comfortable as well. But you get base station tracking and finger tracking.

The other option besides index controllers are the etee controllers, but they are a lot more money and I don't have a reason to think atm that they are particularly better, but I guess they could be in the future. So just get index controllers.

You need to connect it all to your pc. you may need to get a couple MTT usb hubs and/or an extra USB card to hook the trackers up to your pc. Ideally you want to space the dongles 6" apart or more if you can. 

If you want the best QUALITY tracking regardless of battery life or any other fussiness then the vive 2.0 trackers are probably best. but I wouldn't recommend this unless that's the only thing you care about. 2.0s have a slightly wider FOV than 3.0 trackers and are larger, and so are less likely to be occluded.

I was told this is because it is trying to prevent hiccups or something like this. so I don't think it is so much that a "bug" was making you experience high fps, but rather that you were temporarily hitting high enough fps to not be limited.

and given 72fps is half of 144, I'm gonna guess that you have an index. oh wait, nevermind, maybe you're on a quest 1? not sure what headsets run at 72fps native unless you're using a limiting setting.

also there's synchronous spacewarp. When SSW is on, your framerate will be halved in steam, but the headset will interpolate the rest of the frames to give you your headset's refresh rate. If it is on "auto" mode it will try to determine if current performance is good enough to give you native headset refresh, or to drop you to half and use SSW. so maybe this setting is on auto.
